{{Short description|American chemist and historian (born 1937)}}
{{BLP sources|date=October 2024}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=January 2025}}
'''Robert E. Kohler''' (born 1937) is an American chemist and historian of science, specializing in the [[life sciences]].

==Early life and education==
In 1959, Kohler graduated from [[Yale University]] with a B.A. summa cum laude in [[chemistry]].<ref name=HSS>{{cite web|url=https://hss.sas.upenn.edu/people/robert-e-kohler |title=Robert E. Kohler &#124; HSS &#124; Arts & Sciences }}</ref> In 1965, he received his Ph.D. in chemistry from [[Harvard University]].<ref name=papers>{{cite web|url=https://findingaids.library.upenn.edu/records/SCIHIST_2007.509 |title=Robert E. Kohler Papers - Philadelphia Area Archives }}</ref> His Ph.D. thesis is entitled ''Model studies for the synthesis of β-amyrin''.<ref>{{cite web|author=Kohler, Robert E.|title=Model studies for the synthesis of β-amyrin|year=1965|url=https://id.lib.harvard.edu/alma/990068312100203941/catalog|website=Harvard University Library catalog entry}}</ref> From 1965 to 1970 he remained at Harvard as a research fellow, from 1965 to 1968 at [[Harvard Medical School]]'s microbiology department and from 1968 to 1970 at Harvard University's history of science department. From 1970 to 1973 he was assistant director of the [[Burndy Library]], a library founded in 1941 by [[Bern Dibner]]. 

== Career ==
In 1973 he joined the faculty of the [[University of Pennsylvania]]'s department of history and sociology of science,<ref name="papers" /> where he was appointed full professor in 1988 and retired as professor emeritus in 2005.<ref name="PAFA">{{cite web|url=https://www.pafa.org/news/pafa-welcomes-six-new-board-trustee-members |title=PAFA Welcomes Six New Board of Trustee Members &#124; PAFA - Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts |date=14 July 2016 }}</ref> He taught courses on the history of American science, the history of technology in war, [[landscape]] and [[environmental history]], and science as a social practice. In 1995 he was a visiting professor at the [[University of California, San Diego]].<ref name="CV" />

While Kohler wrote his dissertation on the biochemistry of [[Amyrin|beta-amyrin]], he increasingly turned to topics in the history of science. At the University of Pennsylvania, he gained an international reputation for his research on the history of genetics and biochemistry, as well as the [[sociology]] of American science. In his work in 1971/72, he dealt with the background and reception of the discovery of [[cell (biology)|cell-free]] [[fermentation]] by [[Eduard Buchner]], winner of the 1907 [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]]. Kohler later investigated the historical basis of science funding and the history of genetics. In the 1980s he incorporated sociological elements into his studies and showed in 1982 in ''From Medical Chemistry to Biochemistry: The Making of a Biomedical Discipline'' that the discipline of [[biochemistry]] arose from the conflicts over control of medical schools, particularly between clinical practitioners and researchers.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Neuberger, Albert|author-link=Albert Neuberger|title=review of ''From Medical Chemistry to Biochemistry'' by Robert E. Kohler|journal=[[FEBS Letters]]|volume=168|issue=1|page=184|date=March 1984|doi=10.1016/0014-5793(84)80237-9 |url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/82652058.pdf}}</ref> A similar sociological interest led him to investigate the funding mechanisms in the shaping of American science. He published the results in several influential articles and in 1991 in the work ''Partners in Science: Foundations and Natural Scientists, 1900–1945''.<ref>{{cite journal|title=review of ''Partners in Science'' by Robert E. Kohler|author=Owens, Larry|journal=Science|volume=254|issue=5035|pages=1233–1234|date=22 November 1991|doi=10.1126/science.254.5035.1233|pmid=17776417 }} [https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.254.5035.1234 p. 1234]</ref> In the 2000s he worked on the culture and practice of [[biology]] and [[biodiversity]], as well as the history of geographical and biological fieldwork.<ref name=CV>{{cite web|title=Curriculum Vitae: Robert E. Kohler|website=Department of History and Sociology of Science, School of Arts & Sciences, University of Pennsylvania|url=https://hss.sas.upenn.edu/sites/default/files/Kohler%20CV%202018.pdf}} (with comprehensive publication list)</ref>

Robert E. Kohler was an advisory editor from 1984 to 2011 for ''[[Social Studies of Science]]'', from 1987 to 1992 for [[Isis (journal)|''Isis'']], and from 1991 to 2001 of the ''[[Journal of the History of Biology]]''. In 2005 he became an advisory editor for ''[[Nature and Culture]]''. He has published 6 books and more than 30 scientific articles.<ref name=CV/>

In 2004 Kohler received the [[George Sarton Medal]] from the [[History of Science Society]] (HSS).<ref>{{cite journal|author=Nyhart, Lynn K.|author-link=Lynn K. Nyhart|title=Sarton Medal 2004, Robert Kohler, HSS 2004 Prize Citations|date=5 November 2009|doi=10.1086/501106 |journal=Isis |volume=97 |pages=133–139 }}</ref> In 2016 he was elected to the board of trustee of the [[Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts]] (PAFA).<ref name=PAFA/>

==Personal life==
On June 6, 1958, Robert E. Kohler married Frances Coulborn (1938–2021). As an editor and manager, she contributed to the success of the history of science journals ''[[Isis (journal)|Isis]]'' and [[Osiris (journal)|''Osiris'']]. She was director of publications for the [[Chemical Heritage Foundation]].<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1086/722357 |title=Eloge: Frances Coulborn Kohler (1938–2021) |date=2022 |last1=Kohler |first1=Robert E. |last2=Nyhart |first2=Lynn K. |last3=Thackray |first3=Arnold |journal=Isis |volume=113 |issue=4 |pages=841–846 }}</ref> Upon her death she was survived by her widower, two sons, and three grandchildren.<ref>{{cite web|title=Obituary. Frances Coulborn (1938–2021)|website=olearyfuneral.com|url=https://www.olearyfuneral.com/obituary/Frances-Kohler}}</ref> Frances Kohler was a friend of Wilma Anderson Kerby-Miller.<ref>{{cite web|title=Letter from Frances Coulborn Kohler to James D. Watson|website=CSHL Archives Repository|url=https://aceserver.cshl.org/items/show/33629}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Wilma Anderson Kerby-Miller|website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences|date=9 February 2023 |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/wilma-anderson-kerby-miller}}</ref>
